title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 350
paragraphs: As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having arrived there to practice her trade, she was ransomed from slavery for a large sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos, the brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus Rhodopis was set free, and she remained in Egypt, and by her beauty she won so much favor that she made a great deal of money — great for someone like Rhodopis — though not enough to cover the cost of such a pyramid as this. In fact, there is no need to credit her with very great wealth, since the tithe of her wealth can still be seen even now by anyone who wants to look. For Rhodopis wished to leave behind in Hellas a memorial of herself — something that no one else had thought of or dedicated in a temple — and to offer it at Delphi as her memorial. Accordingly, with the tithe of her wealth she had iron spits made, large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far as her tithe allowed. She sent them to Delphi, and they are still lying there today, heaped together behind the altar the Chians dedicated, directly opposite the inner sanctum of the temple. As it happens, the courtesans at Naucratis tend to win renown, for this woman first, about whom this story is told, became so famous that every Greek without exception came to know the name of Rhodopis; and after her, one named Archidiche was sung about throughout Hellas, though she was less talked about than the former. As for Charaxos, after ransoming Rhodopis and returning to Mytilene, he was savagely abused by Sappho in an ode. About Rhodopis, then, I will say no more.
